strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant limitation of 3D Gaussian Splatting: rendering-time memory, which is more consequential for deployment than compressed file size alone.

Replacing spherical harmonics with arbitrarily oriented spherical-Gaussian lobes is well motivated. It provides an adjustable per-primitive representation and appears to offer a favorable quality-memory trade-off.
The evaluation covers three established dataset families and a reasonably broad collection of pruning, coefficient-reduction, vector-quantization, neural-compression, and anchor-based baselines.

The reported results are promising: MEGS2 substantially reduces static and rendering VRAM relative to vanilla 3DGS and GaussianSpa while retaining comparable reconstruction quality. The ablations also examine the SG representation, soft versus hard pruning, unified versus sequential pruning, and color compensation.
Separating static and dynamic rendering memory is a useful perspective, and the paper clearly explains why storage-oriented compression does not necessarily reduce deployment memory.
weaknesses: The central claim of unified memory-constrained optimization is not fully supported by the stated algorithm. Although Eq. 6 defines one weighted joint budget, Eqs. 11-12 factorize its projection into separately selected primitive and lobe budgets, kappa_o and kappa_s. This pre-allocates the trade-off instead of jointly optimizing it, and the paper neither specifies how these budgets are chosen nor proves that the factorized operation solves the original projection. The update equations in Algorithm 1 also omit the rho weights appearing in Eqs. 7-8.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Crucial details are missing, including the initial number of lobes, total and split budgets, penalty schedule, pruning thresholds, number of sparse-training and fine-tuning steps, proximal-operator choices by scene, and enforcement of lobe-axis and sharpness constraints. No code or resource availability statement is provided.

The memory-measurement protocol is underspecified. Reporting PyTorch values does not establish whether allocated or reserved memory is measured, how peaks and synchronization are handled, whether caches are reset, or which image resolution and renderer settings are used. Several baseline VRAM values are estimated rather than directly measured, and no uncertainty or repeated-run statistics are given.

The headline edge-device claim is weakly evaluated. Figure 1 reports FPS on three devices, but the paper gives no detailed WebGL implementation, scene and resolution settings, memory measurements, precision choices, or controlled comparison. All substantive experiments are conducted on an RTX 3090, so the claimed mobile applicability is not convincingly established.

Table 1 contains two unlabeled rows for the proposed method, apparently corresponding to different compression budgets. This makes a central quantitative result ambiguous. Results are also reported mainly as dataset averages without per-scene breakdowns, quality-memory curves, or variability.

The novelty is moderate rather than decisive: spherical Gaussians have already been used for Gaussian splatting, while constrained opacity pruning and ADMM-inspired sparsification build directly on GaussianSpa. The main novelty is their combination with lobe pruning, but the strongest claim—that this combination performs genuinely joint budget allocation—is precisely where the formulation is incomplete.

The budget counts scalar parameters rather than actual device memory and does not explicitly couple primitive removal to removal of that primitive's lobes. Variable-length storage, indexing, alignment, and renderer-specific overhead can therefore make the theoretical constraint diverge from realized VRAM.

The paper overstates its conclusions with phrases such as 'fundamentally solves' and 'globally optimal memory footprint.' Neither global optimality nor a general solution to dynamic rendering memory is demonstrated; the limitations section explicitly acknowledges that dynamic memory is not part of the optimization objective.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck: rendering-time memory, rather than only compressed file size, for 3D Gaussian Splatting.

Replacing spherical harmonics with learnable, arbitrarily oriented spherical-Gaussian lobes is intuitive and yields a flexible per-primitive representation whose complexity can be reduced by pruning lobes.
The reported results show substantial static and rendering VRAM reductions, with generally competitive PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS across three established novel-view-synthesis datasets.

The paper compares against several relevant pruning and compression baselines and includes ablations for color representation, soft versus hard pruning, sequential versus unified pruning, and color compensation.
The distinction between static and dynamic rendering memory is useful, and the paper is generally readable with informative qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: The central claim of unified memory-constrained optimization is not supported by the presented algorithm. Equation 6 imposes one joint weighted budget, but Equations 11–12 factorize its projection into separately chosen budgets κ_o and κ_s. No rule relating these budgets to κ is given, and this factorization cannot generally find the optimal allocation between primitives and lobes. The method therefore appears closer to jointly trained but separately budgeted pruning than to the claimed unified constrained optimization.

The stated memory model is internally inconsistent. A surviving primitive requires position, rotation, scale, opacity, and the three-parameter diffuse color, totaling 14 base float parameters, yet ρ_o is set to 11. Table 2 separately confirms that the diffuse color contributes three parameters. Moreover, lobes belonging to a removed primitive should not incur memory, so the additive independent L0 expression does not precisely represent the deployed model's memory.

Important mathematical and implementation details are missing. The paper does not specify how κ_o and κ_s are selected, how opacity projections are chosen for each scene, the pruning thresholds, key penalty and optimization schedules, or how nonnegative sharpness and unit-length lobe axes are enforced. The range criterion in Equation 13 also produces an RGB-valued quantity unless a norm or channel aggregation is specified.

Table 1 contains two unlabeled rows under “Ours,” apparently corresponding to different budgets. Their configurations are never identified, making the main comparisons and claimed compression ratios ambiguous. The evaluation also reports no repeated-run variation or statistical uncertainty.

The VRAM methodology is insufficiently controlled and reproducible. It does not clarify whether allocated or reserved PyTorch memory is used, how framework overhead is removed, or the exact rendering resolution and synchronization protocol. Some baseline VRAM values are estimated rather than measured, while different representations and decoding implementations are compared. Table 3 further reports a single undefined VRAM quantity despite the paper's emphasis on separating static and rendering memory.

Claims about enabling edge-device rendering are weakly substantiated. Nearly all controlled experiments use an RTX 3090; the mobile results in Figure 1 omit scene, model size, resolution, quality settings, memory use, and measurement protocol. Vanilla 3DGS is merely marked unavailable on mobile, and there is no comparison against mobile-oriented implementations. Comprehensive latency, power, and thermal measurements are absent.

The novelty is moderate: spherical Gaussians have already been used for 3DGS, and the constrained sparsification machinery largely builds on GaussianSpa. Given that the supposedly novel unified projection is actually factorized, the conceptual advance over combining SG color modeling with existing sparsification is unclear.

Several conclusions are overstated. The experiments do not establish that the method “fundamentally solves” the memory bottleneck, achieves a globally optimal footprint, or creates a new compression paradigm. Dynamic memory is explicitly excluded from the optimization, complex highlights are not thoroughly tested, and training-time memory and cost are not reported.

No code or sufficiently detailed pseudocode/configuration is provided to resolve the ambiguities above, substantially limiting reproducibility. Overall, the promising empirical direction does not compensate for the mismatch between the central formulation and algorithm and the under-specified evaluation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant limitation of 3D Gaussian Splatting: rendering-time memory, which is more consequential for deployment than compressed file size alone.

Replacing spherical harmonics with arbitrarily oriented spherical Gaussian lobes is intuitive and effective. The experiments indicate a favorable quality-memory trade-off, especially after lobe pruning.

The empirical results are promising across Mip-NeRF360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending. MEGS 2 attains quality comparable to or better than strong lightweight baselines while reporting roughly 50% lower static VRAM and 40% lower rendering VRAM than GaussianSpa.

The comparison covers several relevant method families, including primitive pruning, SH reduction, vector quantization, neural compression, and anchor-based compression. The authors also directly reproduce multiple baselines for memory measurement.

The ablations address the main design choices—SG color modeling, soft versus hard pruning, unified versus sequential pruning, and color compensation—and the qualitative examples generally support the quantitative results.
weaknesses: The central claim of a unified total-memory-constrained optimization is not fully supported by the described algorithm. Although Eq. 6 defines one joint budget, Eqs. 11–12 factorize the projection into separately chosen primitive and lobe budgets. This removes the mechanism by which the optimizer would jointly allocate a global budget between primitives and lobes, undermining claims of a globally optimal trade-off.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the values or schedules for the total and factorized budgets, ADMM penalty, pruning thresholds, number of sparse-training and fine-tuning steps, and rules for selecting proximal operators. No code or explicit release commitment is stated.

The edge-deployment motivation is insufficiently evaluated. Most experiments use an RTX 3090; the mobile FPS claims in Figure 1 lack scene, resolution, quality, memory, and implementation details. There are no systematic mobile-device comparisons against deployable baselines.

Table 1 contains two unlabeled rows for the proposed method, apparently corresponding to different compression levels, without explaining their configurations. This makes a major headline comparison ambiguous.

The memory protocol needs greater rigor. The paper averages per-view peak memory reported by PyTorch, but does not report variance, absolute device baselines, allocator settings, or an independent measurement. Some baseline memory values are estimated rather than measured, limiting comparability.

The reported ablation does not establish a controlled Pareto frontier. For example, the sequential and unified variants have different VRAM footprints, so their quality difference does not isolate the benefit of unified optimization at a matched budget.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence, including that the method “fundamentally solves” the memory bottleneck, provides “globally optimal” memory allocation, or establishes a new paradigm. Dynamic rendering memory is not included in the optimization, despite accounting for much of the measured footprint.
